name: Yardi Aspire
toolCategory: Learning management system built by a property management software vendor, sold with its own real estate course library

verdict.line: The most credible head-to-head LMS in the category — it has real multifamily content, state-approved fair housing, 100+ Spanish courses and AI authoring, so win on outcome proof (competency, shops, surveys, benchmarks) rather than on feature checklists.

size.value: Over 9,000 professionals in more than 40 offices worldwide (company-wide, not Aspire-specific)

pricing.value: Not published. Three named tiers exist — Aspire, Aspire Plus and Aspire Platinum.

positioning.value: Positions Aspire as an advanced online learning tool that centralizes training, policies and resources in a single mobile-friendly hub to activate employee potential across onboarding, compliance and performance.

strengths.text: State-approved fair housing content: fair housing courses approved by TDHCA and the Florida DBPR that qualify for continuing education credit.
State-variant harassment prevention course pages for California, Connecticut, New York, Maine and Illinois, with stated ongoing regulatory updates.
More than 100 bilingual English/Spanish courses plus Canadian French options.
AI content-generation tooling that builds interactive courses, scenario challenges, assessments and translations inside the authoring environment.
Single sign-on across the Yardi ecosystem via YardiOne, making it low-friction for existing Voyager clients.
Supports NAA credential maintenance (CAM, CAPS, CALP).

gaps.text: Capability is split across three purchase tiers — SCORM compatibility, embedded e-signature, live polling and Microsoft Teams integration are named as Platinum-tier features, so the base tier is not the same product.
No benchmarking of training performance against an industry dataset is described on the Aspire product page or the published course catalog overview.
The published catalog does not state a total course count, so library depth cannot be compared line-for-line from public sources.
Fair housing state approvals named publicly are Texas (TDHCA) and Florida (DBPR); no broader multi-state fair housing approval list is published.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill measures competency, not just completion — tie the conversation to what the team can demonstrate, not what they clicked through.
Aspire proves training happened; PerformanceHQ connects training to mystery shop scores, resident and employee survey results and reputation signals in one place.
Aspire's published fair housing state approvals are Texas and Florida — for a multi-state portfolio, ask how each additional jurisdiction is covered.
Capability is tiered (Aspire / Plus / Platinum) — confirm which tier the quoted price actually buys before comparing features.
askThis: Which Aspire tier is in the quote — base, Plus or Platinum? Which of the features you were shown are Platinum-only?
For the states your portfolio operates in beyond Texas and Florida, what fair housing approval or jurisdiction variant is provided?
How do you know a leasing consultant can actually do the thing, versus that they finished the course?
How would you compare your training completion against what the rest of the industry is doing?
If your organization moves off Yardi Voyager, what happens to the training system and the completion history?

objections.objection: It's already in our Yardi stack, so it's simpler.
objections.response: Single sign-on is real and worth something. The question is what the content does after login — ask which tier you're on, which states are covered, and whether you can show competency rather than completion.

objections.objection: Yardi has AI course creation now.
objections.response: Authoring speed is a content-production feature. Our value is the content already being written, maintained and jurisdiction-current, plus the ability to connect what people learned to what happened at the property.

objections.objection: Yardi has Spanish content too.
objections.response: Agreed — that's a genuine strength on their side. Take the comparison to depth and currency: which courses are bilingual, and who updates them when regulation changes.

doNotSay: They don't have fair housing content — they do, with published Texas and Florida approvals.
They don't have Spanish content — they publish 100+ bilingual courses.
They can't do SCORM — SCORM compatibility is named in the Platinum tier.
Any claim about Aspire's price, customer count or course count — none is published.

verdict.line: Same buyer, same budget line, already inside a stack they own — but RealPage publishes far less about content depth, fair housing and compliance reporting than we do, so make the conversation about what is actually in the library and how compliance is proven.

positioning.value: Describes RealConnect as removing barriers to learning, enhancing the learning experience and establishing learning as a culture to activate employees' potential, with 360-degree content coverage across multifamily soft skills, RealPage product training and custom-created training.

strengths.text: Distributed inside an installed platform base — for existing RealPage clients it is an add-on to an incumbent vendor relationship, not a new procurement.
Mobile-first design explicitly built for just-in-time access on mobile devices.

Fully translated English and Spanish learner interface.

toolCategory: Multifamily-native online course library and LMS, sold standalone and bundled with its parent's property management products

verdict.line: A genuine multifamily content competitor with 300+ short courses and named state accreditations, usually discounted into an Inhabit bundle — compete on breadth of compliance coverage, competency evidence and the ability to connect training to operational outcomes.

ownership.value: Owned by Inhabit, a global PropTech company whose brands include ResMan, ResidentIQ, ValenceDocs, Anyone Home, Streamline and others

size.value: Inhabit reports 1,100+ employees worldwide (parent company, not GROW-specific)

pricing.value: Not published. Four purchase models described: a la carte individual courses, bundle with partner Inhabit products (ValenceDocs, APTEXX, Nationwide Compliant, AMS Billing), subscription to the full 300+ course catalog, and one-time SCORM purchase for use in a client's own LMS.

positioning.value: "GROW brings your workplace culture to life by offering short, engaging, relevant courses resulting in productive, valued, happy employees" — training for multifamily and short-term rental property management.

strengths.text: Catalog of over 300 courses spanning 28+ topic areas including leasing, maintenance, operations, fair housing and resident retention.
Named state accreditations: fair housing accredited in Texas and Virginia; human trafficking content meeting Florida and California requirements; Asbestos Class IV aligned to EPA and OSHA standards.
Courses available in SCORM format for one-time purchase and delivery inside a client's existing LMS — a low-commitment entry point that can displace a full platform sale.
Doubles as a company intranet and customizable dashboard, not only a course player.
Custom course development by property management professionals plus upload of a client's existing materials.
Bundleable with Inhabit sibling products, giving the parent a discounting lever in competitive deals.

gaps.text: Published fair housing accreditation covers two states (Texas and Virginia); no broader multi-state approval list is published.
GROW's public site does not describe CEC/credential eligibility (CAM, CAPS, CALP), Spanish or bilingual content, assessments/competency measurement, HRIS integration, or benchmarking.
The customizable-training page describes upload and custom development but does not describe SCORM import, assessment authoring, role-based assignment mechanics or reporting detail.
Branding is fragmented across the parent's estate — the same learning capability is presented as GROW, as ResidentIQ Learning Management and as ResMan Learning depending on the entry point.

whyWeWin: Multi-state portfolios need jurisdiction coverage beyond two states — ask what happens in every state GROW does not publish an accreditation for.
Short courses averaging minutes are good for engagement and weak for proof; ask what evidence exists that someone can do the job, not that they watched the video.
GROW publishes no Spanish/bilingual content claim — if the workforce is bilingual, that is a concrete, checkable difference.
Training that isn't connected to shops, surveys and reputation data can't tell you whether it worked.
askThis: Which states beyond Texas and Virginia are covered for fair housing, and who signs off that the content is current?
How much of the catalog is available in Spanish?
Do the courses carry CEC credit toward CAM, CAPS or CALP?
What does the assessment look like — is there a score, and does it gate anything?
Are you buying the platform or one-time SCORM files? What happens to your completion history in the SCORM model?
If the training bundle is priced against other Inhabit products, what happens to that price if you change any one of them?

objections.objection: GROW has 300+ courses, that's plenty.
objections.response: Course count and coverage aren't the same. Ask how many are fair housing, which states they're accredited in, and how many exist in Spanish — that's where the gap shows up.

objections.objection: We can just buy the SCORM files and run them in our own LMS.
objections.response: That works until the regulation changes. Ask who is responsible for updating a SCORM file you already bought and loaded — and how you'd know it went stale.

objections.objection: It's bundled with our Inhabit products at a good price.
objections.response: Bundle pricing is real leverage on their side. Make sure the comparison is apples-to-apples on jurisdiction coverage and competency evidence before it turns into a price conversation.

doNotSay: GROW has no fair housing content — they publish accreditation in Texas and Virginia.
They have no Spanish content — it is unverified, not disproven.

That GROW and ResMan Learning are definitively the same product — public sources present them as sibling offerings under Inhabit but do not confirm a shared platform.

name: Wranx
toolCategory: Spaced-repetition microlearning reinforcement app — short daily drills on top of training someone else supplies

verdict.line: A knowledge-retention layer, not a training system — no multifamily content and no published compliance coverage, so it reinforces what a buyer already has rather than replacing it.

positioning.value: Positions itself around helping organizations "ditch dull training and build learning habits that drive real results" using spaced repetition — a learning technique for long-term knowledge retention — delivered as roughly two-minute daily drills.

strengths.text: Built entirely on spaced repetition for long-term knowledge retention — a defensible pedagogical differentiator most LMS vendors do not claim.
Extremely low time cost per learner — daily drills of roughly two minutes, which suits high-turnover frontline teams.
AI Content Builder rapidly generates quizzes from a customer's existing materials.
Established since 2014 with named enterprise clients including The North Face, DFIN, Renault and Cunard.
Analytics and performance reporting on knowledge retention over time, not just completion.

gaps.text: Named industries served are retail, utilities and hospitality; multifamily and property management are not mentioned and no multifamily client is named.
The About page does not describe a vendor-supplied course library — the content model is built around a customer's existing materials via the AI Content Builder.
The About page does not specify mobile app details, offline functionality, SCORM compliance, language support, integrations or pricing.
No fair housing, state-specific compliance or CEC/credential content is described.
UK-headquartered with no published US multifamily presence or US regulatory content.

whyWeWin: Wranx reinforces knowledge someone else created — it does not supply fair housing, state compliance or multifamily role content.
Two-minute quizzes are a retention mechanism, not a compliance record; ask what an auditor would accept.
No published US multifamily clients or US regulatory content, and the company is UK-based.
If a prospect likes the retention idea, position Grace Hill's competency assessment as the same instinct applied to content that already exists and is maintained.
askThis: Where would the fair housing content come from — Wranx builds quizzes from material you already have.
Do you have a US multifamily reference we can speak with?
If you're audited on training completion, is a quiz streak the record you'd want to produce?
Are the drills available in Spanish?
Does it work offline for maintenance techs who lose signal in a basement?

objections.objection: Spaced repetition actually makes training stick — that's better than another LMS.
objections.response: The learning science is real and worth respecting. It's a reinforcement layer though: it needs source content, and for multifamily that content is the expensive, regulated part.

objections.objection: It's two minutes a day, our teams will actually do it.
objections.response: Engagement is a genuine strength. The question to settle first is whether daily quizzes satisfy your compliance obligation — usually you'll need both.

doNotSay: Wranx doesn't work / isn't a real platform — it has been operating since 2014 with named enterprise clients.
They have no content at all — the About page doesn't describe a course library, which is not the same as confirming none exists.
